# Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, First Part

**Theorem.** Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the closed real interval $[a,b]$, and let $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by
$$F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm dt .$$
Then $F$ is a primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$; that is, $F$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ (the derivative being the appropriate one-sided derivative at the endpoints $a$ and $b$) and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in[a,b].$$

The claim as stated is **true**, and is proved below. Throughout, $[a,b]$ is a non-degenerate closed real interval, i.e. $a<b$. (If one allows $a=b$, then $[a,b]=\{a\}$ is a single point, at which no difference quotient can be formed, and the assertion is vacuous.)

The proof has two ingredients: (i) the integral defining $F$ exists, and behaves additively over adjacent subintervals, so that $F(y)-F(x)=\int_x^y f$; and (ii) on a short interval around $x$, continuity pins $f$ to within $\varepsilon$ of $f(x)$, so $\int_x^{x+h} f$ is within $\varepsilon|h|$ of $h\,f(x)$.

---

## 0. Definitions, conventions, and the standard facts used

### 0.1 The integral

We use the Darboux formulation of the Riemann integral (equivalent to Riemann's own definition; we shall not need that equivalence).

Let $u<v$ and let $g:[u,v]\to\mathbb{R}$ be **bounded**. A *partition* of $[u,v]$ is a finite set $P=\{t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n\}$ with
$$u=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=v .$$
Writing, for $1\le i\le n$,
$$m_i(g,P)=\inf_{t\in[t_{i-1},t_i]}g(t),\qquad M_i(g,P)=\sup_{t\in[t_{i-1},t_i]}g(t)$$
(these exist in $\mathbb{R}$ because $g$ is bounded), the *lower* and *upper Darboux sums* are
$$L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_i(g,P)\,(t_i-t_{i-1}),\qquad U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}M_i(g,P)\,(t_i-t_{i-1}),$$
and the *lower* and *upper integrals* are
$$\underline{\int_u^v}g=\sup_{P}L(g,P),\qquad \overline{\int_u^v}g=\inf_{P}U(g,P),$$
the supremum and infimum being over all partitions $P$ of $[u,v]$. We say $g$ is *(Darboux–Riemann) integrable* on $[u,v]$ iff these two numbers are equal, and then $\int_u^v g(t)\,\mathrm dt$ denotes their common value. For a degenerate interval we use the usual convention
$$\int_u^u g(t)\,\mathrm dt=0 .$$

We record the standard elementary facts we shall use.

**(F1) (Refinement.)** If $P\subseteq Q$ are partitions of $[u,v]$, then
$$L(g,P)\le L(g,Q)\qquad\text{and}\qquad U(g,Q)\le U(g,P).$$

*Reason.* By induction on $\#(Q\setminus P)$ it suffices to treat $Q=P\cup\{p\}$ with $t_{i-1}<p<t_i$ for some $i$. All terms of $L(g,P)$ and $L(g,Q)$ agree except that the term $m_i(t_i-t_{i-1})$ of $L(g,P)$ is replaced in $L(g,Q)$ by
$$\Bigl(\inf_{[t_{i-1},p]}g\Bigr)(p-t_{i-1})+\Bigl(\inf_{[p,t_i]}g\Bigr)(t_i-p).$$
Since $[t_{i-1},p]$ and $[p,t_i]$ are subsets of $[t_{i-1},t_i]$, both of those infima are $\ge m_i$, so the replacement term is $\ge m_i\bigl((p-t_{i-1})+(t_i-p)\bigr)=m_i(t_i-t_{i-1})$. Hence $L(g,P)\le L(g,Q)$. The statement for $U$ is symmetric (suprema over subsets are $\le M_i$). $\square$

**(F2)** For any partitions $P,Q$ of $[u,v]$ we have $L(g,P)\le U(g,Q)$; consequently $\underline{\int_u^v}g\le\overline{\int_u^v}g$, and both are finite.

*Reason.* For a single partition $R$, $m_i(g,R)\le M_i(g,R)$ for each $i$ gives $L(g,R)\le U(g,R)$. Applying this to $R=P\cup Q$ and using (F1),
$$L(g,P)\le L(g,R)\le U(g,R)\le U(g,Q).$$
Thus $U(g,Q)$ is an upper bound for $\{L(g,P)\}_P$, whence $\underline{\int}g\le U(g,Q)$ for every $Q$, whence $\underline{\int}g\le\overline{\int}g$. Finiteness: if $|g|\le K$ then $-K(v-u)\le L(g,P),U(g,P)\le K(v-u)$ for all $P$. $\square$

**(F3) (Riemann's criterion; the direction we need.)** If $g$ is bounded on $[u,v]$ and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a partition $P_\varepsilon$ of $[u,v]$ with $U(g,P_\varepsilon)-L(g,P_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon$, then $g$ is integrable on $[u,v]$.

*Reason.* By definition and (F2), for each $\varepsilon>0$,
$$0\le\overline{\int_u^v}g-\underline{\int_u^v}g\le U(g,P_\varepsilon)-L(g,P_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon .$$
A non-negative real number smaller than every $\varepsilon>0$ is $0$. $\square$

### 0.2 Facts about continuous functions

**(F4) (Extreme Value Theorem.)** If $u\le v$ and $g:[u,v]\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g$ is bounded on $[u,v]$ and attains a maximum and a minimum value there.

**(F5) (Heine–Cantor.)** If $u\le v$ and $g:[u,v]\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g$ is uniformly continuous on $[u,v]$: for every $\eta>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|g(s)-g(t)|<\eta$ whenever $s,t\in[u,v]$ and $|s-t|<\delta$.

Both are standard consequences of the compactness (equivalently, the Heine–Borel or Bolzano–Weierstrass property) of a closed bounded real interval.

We also use the trivial remark that the restriction of a continuous function to a subinterval is continuous on that subinterval; hence $f$ is continuous on every $[u,v]\subseteq[a,b]$, and (F4), (F5) apply to $f$ on every such subinterval.

### 0.3 Continuity on an interval, and primitives

*$f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$* means: for each $x\in[a,b]$ and each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$$t\in[a,b]\ \text{and}\ |t-x|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon .$$
(This is continuity relative to $[a,b]$; at $x=a$ and $x=b$ it amounts to one-sided continuity.)

*$F$ is a primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$* means: $F$ is differentiable at each $x\in[a,b]$ with $F'(x)=f(x)$, where the derivative at $x$ is understood relative to $[a,b]$, i.e.
$$F'(x):=\lim_{\substack{h\to0,\ h\ne0\\ x+h\in[a,b]}}\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h},$$
which for $x=a$ is the right-hand derivative and for $x=b$ the left-hand derivative. Explicitly, $F'(x)=\ell$ means: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$$0<|h|<\delta\ \text{and}\ x+h\in[a,b]\ \Longrightarrow\ \left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-\ell\right|<\varepsilon .$$
(Since $a<b$, for every $x\in[a,b]$ the set of admissible $h$ meets every punctured neighbourhood of $0$, so this limit is well posed and unique.)

---

## 1. Three lemmas

### Lemma A (a continuous function is integrable)

*Let $u<v$ and let $g:[u,v]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Then $g$ is integrable on $[u,v]$.*

**Proof.** By (F4), $g$ is bounded on $[u,v]$, so all Darboux sums are defined.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Apply (F5) with $\eta=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)}>0$: there is $\delta>0$ such that
$$s,t\in[u,v],\ |s-t|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |g(s)-g(t)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)} . \tag{A.1}$$
Choose $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $n\ge1$, with $\dfrac{v-u}{n}<\delta$ (possible by the Archimedean property), and let $P=\{t_0,t_1,\dots,t_n\}$ where $t_i=u+i\,\dfrac{v-u}{n}$. This is a partition of $[u,v]$, and each subinterval $[t_{i-1},t_i]$ has length $\dfrac{v-u}{n}<\delta$.

Fix $i$. By (F4) applied to $g$ on $[t_{i-1},t_i]$ there are $r_i,s_i\in[t_{i-1},t_i]$ with
$$g(r_i)=\min_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g=m_i(g,P),\qquad g(s_i)=\max_{[t_{i-1},t_i]}g=M_i(g,P).$$
Since $r_i,s_i\in[t_{i-1},t_i]\subseteq[u,v]$ and $|s_i-r_i|\le t_i-t_{i-1}<\delta$, (A.1) gives
$$M_i(g,P)-m_i(g,P)=g(s_i)-g(r_i)\le|g(s_i)-g(r_i)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)} .$$
Therefore
$$U(g,P)-L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(M_i(g,P)-m_i(g,P)\bigr)(t_i-t_{i-1})\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(t_i-t_{i-1})=\frac{\varepsilon}{2(v-u)}(v-u)=\frac\varepsilon2<\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, (F3) shows that $g$ is integrable on $[u,v]$. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary A.1 ($F$ is well defined).** For every $x\in[a,b]$ the integral $\int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm dt$ exists; hence $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is a well-defined real function, and $F(a)=0$. Indeed, for $x=a$ this is the convention $\int_a^a f=0$, and for $x>a$ the function $f$ is continuous on $[a,x]\subseteq[a,b]$, so Lemma A applies. The same argument shows $\int_u^v f(t)\,\mathrm dt$ exists for every $u,v$ with $a\le u\le v\le b$.

### Lemma B (crude bounds for an integral)

*Let $u<v$, let $g$ be integrable on $[u,v]$, and let $m,M\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ for all $t\in[u,v]$. Then*
$$m\,(v-u)\ \le\ \int_u^v g(t)\,\mathrm dt\ \le\ M\,(v-u).$$

**Proof.** Consider the trivial partition $P_0=\{u,v\}$ (a partition, since $u<v$). It has the single subinterval $[u,v]$, so
$$L(g,P_0)=\Bigl(\inf_{[u,v]}g\Bigr)(v-u),\qquad U(g,P_0)=\Bigl(\sup_{[u,v]}g\Bigr)(v-u).$$
Since $m$ is a lower bound and $M$ an upper bound for $g$ on $[u,v]$, we have $\inf_{[u,v]}g\ge m$ and $\sup_{[u,v]}g\le M$; as $v-u>0$, this gives $L(g,P_0)\ge m(v-u)$ and $U(g,P_0)\le M(v-u)$. Finally, by the definitions of $\underline\int,\overline\int$ and integrability,
$$L(g,P_0)\le\underline{\int_u^v}g=\int_u^v g(t)\,\mathrm dt=\overline{\int_u^v}g\le U(g,P_0).$$
Combining the displayed inequalities yields the claim. $\blacksquare$

### Lemma C (additivity over adjacent intervals)

*Let $a\le u\le c\le v\le b$. Then all three integrals below exist and*
$$\int_u^v f(t)\,\mathrm dt=\int_u^c f(t)\,\mathrm dt+\int_c^v f(t)\,\mathrm dt .$$

**Proof.** Existence is Corollary A.1.

If $c=u$, the right-hand side is $0+\int_u^v f=\int_u^v f$; if $c=v$, it is $\int_u^v f+0$. (Both use the convention $\int_p^p f=0$.) If $u=v$ then necessarily $u=c=v$ and both sides are $0$. So we may assume $u<c<v$.

Let $\mathcal P$, $\mathcal P_1$, $\mathcal P_2$ denote the sets of partitions of $[u,v]$, $[u,c]$, $[c,v]$ respectively, and let $\mathcal P^c=\{P\in\mathcal P: c\in P\}$.

**(i) A bijection.** If $P\in\mathcal P^c$, then $P_1:=P\cap[u,c]$ is a finite subset of $[u,c]$ containing $u$ and $c$, hence $P_1\in\mathcal P_1$; similarly $P_2:=P\cap[c,v]\in\mathcal P_2$; and $P=P_1\cup P_2$. Conversely, if $P_1\in\mathcal P_1$ and $P_2\in\mathcal P_2$, then $P:=P_1\cup P_2\in\mathcal P^c$, and it recovers $P_1,P_2$ by intersection (because $P_1\subseteq[u,c]$, $P_2\subseteq[c,v]$ and $P_1\cap[c,v]=\{c\}=P_2\cap[u,c]$). So $P\mapsto(P_1,P_2)$ is a bijection $\mathcal P^c\to\mathcal P_1\times\mathcal P_2$.

**(ii) Sums split.** If $P\in\mathcal P^c$ corresponds to $(P_1,P_2)$, then the list of subintervals determined by $P$ is exactly the list of subintervals determined by $P_1$ followed by those determined by $P_2$ (the point $c$ being a division point of $P$). Hence, term by term,
$$L(f,P)=L(f,P_1)+L(f,P_2). \tag{C.1}$$

**(iii) Restricting to partitions containing $c$ is harmless.** For any $P\in\mathcal P$ we have $P\cup\{c\}\in\mathcal P^c$ and, by (F1), $L(f,P)\le L(f,P\cup\{c\})$. Hence every element of $\{L(f,P):P\in\mathcal P\}$ is dominated by an element of $\{L(f,P):P\in\mathcal P^c\}$, while the latter set is contained in the former. Therefore the two sets have the same supremum:
$$\underline{\int_u^v}f=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}L(f,P)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P^c}L(f,P). \tag{C.2}$$

**(iv) Conclusion.** Put $A=\{L(f,P_1):P_1\in\mathcal P_1\}$ and $B=\{L(f,P_2):P_2\in\mathcal P_2\}$. These are non-empty sets of reals, bounded above by (F2) (applied on $[u,c]$ and on $[c,v]$; note $f$ is bounded on $[a,b]$ by (F4)). For non-empty sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ bounded above one has $\sup(A+B)=\sup A+\sup B$, where $A+B=\{\alpha+\beta:\alpha\in A,\beta\in B\}$. [Indeed $\alpha+\beta\le\sup A+\sup B$ for all $\alpha\in A,\beta\in B$, so $\sup(A+B)\le\sup A+\sup B$; and given $\varepsilon>0$, choosing $\alpha>\sup A-\varepsilon/2$, $\beta>\sup B-\varepsilon/2$ gives $\sup(A+B)>\sup A+\sup B-\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.] By (i), (ii), $\{L(f,P):P\in\mathcal P^c\}=A+B$, so by (C.2),
$$\underline{\int_u^v}f=\sup(A+B)=\sup A+\sup B=\underline{\int_u^c}f+\underline{\int_c^v}f .$$
By Corollary A.1 all three functions are integrable on the respective intervals, so each lower integral equals the corresponding integral. This is the assertion. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary C.1.** *For all $x,y$ with $a\le x<y\le b$,*
$$F(y)-F(x)=\int_x^y f(t)\,\mathrm dt .$$

**Proof.** Apply Lemma C with $u=a$, $c=x$, $v=y$ (legitimate, since $a\le x\le y\le b$):
$$F(y)=\int_a^y f(t)\,\mathrm dt=\int_a^x f(t)\,\mathrm dt+\int_x^y f(t)\,\mathrm dt=F(x)+\int_x^y f(t)\,\mathrm dt .$$
(When $x=a$ this reads $F(y)=0+\int_a^y f$, which is correct.) Rearranging gives the claim; all quantities are finite real numbers, so the subtraction is legitimate. $\blacksquare$

---

## 2. Proof of the Theorem

By Corollary A.1, $F$ is a well-defined real function on $[a,b]$. Fix $x\in[a,b]$; we prove that $F$ is differentiable at $x$ (relative to $[a,b]$) with derivative $f(x)$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $f$ is continuous at $x$ relative to $[a,b]$, there is $\delta>0$ such that
$$t\in[a,b],\ |t-x|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(t)-f(x)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. \tag{2.1}$$

Let $h$ be any real number with $0<|h|<\delta$ and $x+h\in[a,b]$. We claim
$$\left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)\right|\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}<\varepsilon . \tag{2.2}$$

**Case 1: $h>0$.** Then $a\le x<x+h\le b$, so $[x,x+h]\subseteq[a,b]$ and $x+h-x=h>0$. For every $t\in[x,x+h]$ we have $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|=t-x\le h<\delta$, so by (2.1)
$$f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\ <\ f(t)\ <\ f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\qquad\text{for all }t\in[x,x+h]. \tag{2.3}$$
By Corollary A.1 the function $f$ is integrable on $[x,x+h]$, so Lemma B applies with $m=f(x)-\varepsilon/2$, $M=f(x)+\varepsilon/2$ and gives
$$\left(f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)h\ \le\ \int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,\mathrm dt\ \le\ \left(f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)h .$$
By Corollary C.1 (with the pair $x<x+h$), $\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,\mathrm dt=F(x+h)-F(x)$. Dividing the resulting inequalities by $h>0$ (which preserves their sense) yields
$$f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\ \le\ \frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}\ \le\ f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2},$$
i.e. (2.2).

**Case 2: $h<0$.** Put $k=-h$, so $k>0$, $k=|h|<\delta$, and $a\le x+h=x-k<x\le b$; thus $[x-k,x]\subseteq[a,b]$. For every $t\in[x-k,x]$ we have $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|=x-t\le k<\delta$, so by (2.1)
$$f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\ <\ f(t)\ <\ f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\qquad\text{for all }t\in[x-k,x].$$
As in Case 1, $f$ is integrable on $[x-k,x]$, whose length is $k>0$, so Lemma B gives
$$\left(f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)k\ \le\ \int_{x-k}^{x}f(t)\,\mathrm dt\ \le\ \left(f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)k ,$$
and Corollary C.1 (with the pair $x-k<x$) gives $\int_{x-k}^{x}f(t)\,\mathrm dt=F(x)-F(x-k)$. Dividing by $k>0$,
$$f(x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\ \le\ \frac{F(x)-F(x-k)}{k}\ \le\ f(x)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.$$
Finally, since $x+h=x-k$ and $h=-k$,
$$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac{F(x-k)-F(x)}{-k}=\frac{F(x)-F(x-k)}{k},$$
so the last display is exactly (2.2).

(Note that at least one of the two cases is non-vacuous for each $x$: if $x<b$ then admissible $h>0$ exist, e.g. any $h$ with $0<h<\min\{\delta,b-x\}$; if $x>a$ then admissible $h<0$ exist; and since $a<b$, at least one of $x<b$, $x>a$ holds.)

**Conclusion of the proof.** We have shown: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that for all real $h$ with $0<|h|<\delta$ and $x+h\in[a,b]$,
$$\left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)\right|<\varepsilon .$$
By the definition in §0.3 this says precisely that
$$\lim_{\substack{h\to0,\ h\ne0\\ x+h\in[a,b]}}\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=f(x),$$
i.e. that $F$ is differentiable at $x$ relative to $[a,b]$ with $F'(x)=f(x)$. For $x=a$ only Case 1 can occur, and the limit is the right-hand derivative, so $F'(a^{+})=f(a)$; for $x=b$ only Case 2 can occur, and the limit is the left-hand derivative, so $F'(b^{-})=f(b)$; for $a<x<b$ both cases occur, and the two-sided derivative exists and equals $f(x)$.

Since $x\in[a,b]$ was arbitrary, $F$ is differentiable on the whole of $[a,b]$ and $F'=f$ there. That is, $F$ is a primitive of $f$ on $[a,b]$. $\blacksquare$

---

## 3. Remarks

1. In particular $F$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, since a function differentiable at a point is continuous there (and one-sidedly so at the endpoints).
2. Continuity of $f$ was used in two places: globally on subintervals, to guarantee via Lemma A that the integrals exist, and at the single point $x$, in (2.1). It cannot simply be dropped: for $f=\chi_{[0,1]}$ on $[-1,1]$ (which is bounded with a single discontinuity, hence integrable) one gets $F(x)=\int_{-1}^{x}f=\max\{x,0\}$, which fails to be differentiable at $0$. On the other hand, the argument of §2 is local in $f$'s continuity: granting the standard facts that a function integrable on $[a,b]$ is integrable on every subinterval and that its integral is additive over adjacent subintervals (so that Lemma B and Corollary C.1 remain available), the very same computation proves the sharper local statement: *if $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and continuous at a single point $x_0\in[a,b]$, then $F$ is differentiable at $x_0$ with $F'(x_0)=f(x_0)$.*
